questions.passage: Historians generally associate the rise of the European coffeehouse with the growing availability of coffee in the seventeenth century. Yet several accounts written decades earlier describe urban establishments where merchants, writers, and other educated people gathered for extended conversations about commerce and public affairs. Because these establishments appear to have performed many of the social functions later associated with coffeehouses, some cultural historians maintain that European coffeehouse culture had already begun to develop before coffee itself became widely available.

choices.text: Historians disagree about precisely when coffee became inexpensive enough to be consumed regularly by people outside wealthy European households.
Some seventeenth-century coffeehouses attracted merchants more frequently than they attracted writers or scholars.
The earlier establishments described in the accounts belonged to a widespread European tradition of taverns and meeting houses that had long served as places for commercial and political discussion.
Only a limited number of surviving sixteenth-century accounts describe the activities that took place inside urban establishments.
Coffeehouses eventually became important centers for the circulation of newspapers, pamphlets, and political information.

questions.passage:
The development of distinctive cultural identities in the great trading cities of early modern Europe was due in considerable measure to the interaction between two social tendencies that might at first appear contradictory: the desire of communities to preserve inherited customs and their practical need to accommodate unfamiliar people and practices. Merchants, artisans, migrants, and travelers brought languages, foods, fashions, rituals, and forms of entertainment into cities whose inhabitants already possessed established ideas about proper conduct and collective belonging. The resulting encounters did not simply replace local traditions with foreign ones. Instead, they encouraged communities to become increasingly selective about which customs they preserved, which they modified, and which they adopted. Cultural exchange, therefore, could strengthen awareness of local identity even while altering the practices through which that identity was expressed.

The kind of cultural adaptation encouraged by repeated contact with outsiders depends heavily on social familiarity—the process by which something initially perceived as foreign gradually becomes recognizable within an existing cultural framework. Familiarity can range from simple recognition of an unfamiliar practice to its incorporation into ordinary social life. Movement across this range is rarely immediate. A foreign custom may first appear only in ports, markets, or neighborhoods frequented by travelers; repeated exposure can then reduce its novelty, while merchants, performers, religious authorities, or political institutions may give it meanings intelligible to local inhabitants. Adoption, however, does not necessarily follow familiarity. Communities may become thoroughly acquainted with a custom and nevertheless reject it, or they may accept only those elements that can be reconciled with existing expectations. Thus cultural adaptation involves interpretation as much as imitation. A borrowed style of clothing may be altered to conform to local standards of modesty, for example, while an imported food may acquire associations with status or celebration that it did not possess in its place of origin. What eventually appears to be a local tradition may consequently contain elements whose foreign origins have become socially unimportant.

The processes of familiarity and interpretation combine in markedly different ways among groups situated differently within the same city. Commercial communities and institutions charged with preserving social or ceremonial authority often respond differently to cultural novelty. For merchants, frequent encounters with outsiders can make flexibility advantageous: unfamiliar languages, manners, and preferences become information that can be used to establish trust, recognize opportunities, and maintain relationships across cultural boundaries. Their adoption of foreign practices may therefore be deliberate and outward-looking, though such practices are usually adjusted to local circumstances. Institutions associated with civic ceremony, religious observance, or established social rank face a different problem. Their authority often depends partly on continuity, and innovations may consequently be approached through classification rather than immediate adoption. Yet resistance does not imply isolation. An institution may reject a foreign practice while modifying its own ceremonies in response to the practice’s growing popularity, just as it may absorb an imported element after redefining that element as compatible with established tradition. Merchants thus tend to encounter cultural difference as a field of possibilities, whereas guardians of established customs tend to encounter it as something requiring interpretation and boundaries. Both participate in cultural change, but the forms of change they produce can make one group appear innovative and the other conservative even when each is responding to the same expanding network of cultural exchange.

choices.text: demonstrate that foreign foods were generally adopted first by socially influential groups
illustrate how a borrowed cultural element can acquire a significance different from the one it originally possessed
suggest that communities are more willing to adopt foreign foods than foreign forms of dress
provide evidence that the original meanings of cultural practices are usually forgotten after those practices are adopted
distinguish cultural practices adopted for practical purposes from those adopted for ceremonial purposes

questions.passage: For many years, manufacturers treated excess inventory primarily as evidence of inaccurate sales forecasts: if demand could be predicted more precisely, firms reasoned, fewer unsold goods would accumulate. Some researchers, however, argue that forecasting errors explain only part of the problem. Firms that reward purchasing managers for obtaining large volume discounts may encourage them to order more materials than production requires, while managers evaluated according to product availability may maintain unusually large stocks to avoid shortages. Thus, even substantial improvements in forecasting may fail to reduce inventory unless firms also consider how their internal performance measures influence purchasing decisions.

choices.text: explain why manufacturers have generally been unable to forecast demand accurately
challenge the view that excess inventory can be addressed primarily by improving demand forecasts
argue that volume discounts usually cost manufacturers more than they save
compare two methods manufacturers use to evaluate purchasing managers
demonstrate that shortages are more costly to manufacturers than excess inventory
